entityDossier.whatItIs: The classified addenda -- variously called annexes, schedules, appendices and supplements -- attached to the three annual national security statutes (Intelligence Authorization Act, National Defense Authorization Act, Department of Defense Appropriations Act) and to the committee reports that accompany them. Together with the classified notification channels of 10 U.S.C. 119, they are the legal machinery by which Congress appropriates money and issues binding direction to programs whose existence is not public. No classified annex has ever been published, in any form, redacted or otherwise.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: If a legacy retrieval and reverse-engineering effort has been funded for eight decades, the money moved through this channel, because there is no other channel that both carries the force of law and never surfaces. The annex system is not a leak in oversight; it is a purpose-built container that gives classified direction "the legal status of public law" while keeping it in a safe in a secure room that few members ever enter. Layered on top of it, 10 U.S.C. 119(e) lets the Secretary of Defense strip specified content out of the Special Access Program reports entirely and deliver it to only twelve people -- the chair and ranking member of six bodies. And the statutory backbone that forced annual SAP disclosure at all, 10 U.S.C. 119(a) and (b), was terminated effective December 31, 2021 by a sunset provision Congress itself enacted. David Grusch's sworn answer to the funding question -- "misappropriation of funds and self-fund" -- describes an abuse that this architecture is uniquely well designed to conceal, because the annex records what Congress intended to buy but the public record cannot be reconciled against it.
entityDossier.narrative:
The classified annex is the least glamorous object on this board and the most important. It is the mechanism that makes the rest of the question -- who, where, under what authority, paid for how -- answerable in principle and unanswerable in practice.

Dakota Rudesill, a former Senate Budget Committee staffer and Intelligence Community official, published the only serious empirical study of the practice. His finding: over thirty-six years Congress wrote at least 124 provisions in 68 Public Laws that can reasonably be read to give classified addenda the force of law, and produced at least 271 committee reports carrying classified addenda since 1977. About half of the 124 were incorporation provisions -- statutory text whose entire operative content is a pointer to a document nobody outside the compartment will ever see. The standard formulation appears at Section 102 of virtually every Intelligence Authorization Act: the amounts authorized and the personnel ceilings "are those specified in the classified Schedule of Authorizations." Accompanying report language routinely states that the Schedule "is incorporated by reference in the Act and has the legal status of public law." The Intelligence Community's own top lawyer has agreed with that characterization.

Rudesill is careful, and his carefulness is itself evidence. He notes that nothing is publicly known about the length of any annex -- "An individual addendum could be two pages long, or 20, or 200" -- and that each committee invites members to read the addenda in a secure room, but "few do." He also records that the practice accelerated: Congress wrote more force-of-law annex provisions in 2011-2015 than in the first eight Congresses of the practice combined, from 1977 to 1992. This is the shape of a mechanism that grew because it worked.

The second layer is statutory rather than procedural. 10 U.S.C. 119 is the SAP oversight statute. Subsection (a) requires an annual March 1 report to the six defense committees listing every DoD special access program, with descriptions, milestones, actual costs by year, and estimated costs across a six-year horizon. Subsection (b) requires a February 1 notice and justification for every new SAP. Subsection (f) forbids initiating a SAP until the defense committees are notified and thirty days elapse. On its face this is real oversight.

Subsection (e) is the escape hatch. The Secretary of Defense "may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report" upon determining that inclusion "would adversely affect the national security." When he does, the information and the justification go "jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees" -- twelve members of Congress, no staff specified. DoD Instruction 5205.11 builds the corresponding category into doctrine: a waived SAP is "An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs."

The third layer is the one almost nobody has noticed. The U.S. Code note appended to Section 119 reads: "For termination, effective Dec. 31, 2021, of provisions in subsecs. (a) and (b) of this section requiring submittal of annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328." The annual SAP report and the new-SAP notice -- the two provisions that produced a written, dated, comprehensive inventory of the black budget's program structure -- were swept away by a generic reporting-burden sunset enacted in the FY2017 NDAA. The subsection (e) waiver survives; the reports it was designed to abridge do not.

Against that background, Congress in December 2022 legislated a tell. 50 U.S.C. 3373b(a)(4)(B) -- Section 1673 of the FY2023 NDAA -- requires the Secretary of Defense, within 72 hours, to report to the defense and intelligence committees and to congressional leadership any authorized UAP disclosure that relates to "a restricted access activity, a special access program, or a compartmented access program that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to the congressional defense committees or the congressional intelligence committees." Congress does not write 72-hour tripwires for hypotheticals. The statute is a signed, dated legislative acknowledgment that unreported access programs are a live possibility.

AARO has since conceded, in its own words, one instance: "In 2021, without sufficient justification, the scope of an IC Controlled Access Program was expanded to protect UAP reverse-engineering." AARO adds that the program never recovered or reverse-engineered anything and was disestablished for lack of merit. Set aside the exculpatory half. The admitted half is that a controlled access program was expanded without sufficient justification, in 2021, specifically to protect UAP reverse-engineering -- which is precisely the nesting behavior Grusch described when he said agencies were "nesting UAP activities in conventional SAP/CAP programs ... without appropriate reporting to various oversight authorities."

Finally, the annex logic reappears in the disclosure statute itself. Under Section 1843 of the FY2024 NDAA, a UAP record may be withheld from the National Archives collection when "the original classification authority makes a determination that there is clear and convincing evidence" of enumerated harms. The original classification authority is the agency holding the record. The annex principle -- the withholder judges the withholding -- survived into the law written to end it.

entityDossier.whatItIs: A protected whistleblower complaint and subsequent sworn congressional testimony by David Charles Grusch, a former Air Force officer, National Reconnaissance Office senior intelligence officer and National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency co-lead for UAP analysis, alleging that a multi-decade U.S. crash-retrieval and reverse-engineering program exists, is concealed from Congress, and is sustained by the misappropriation of appropriated funds. The complaint was filed with the Intelligence Community Inspector General in May 2022 by Charles McCullough III, the first Senate-confirmed ICIG.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: This is the only allegation of its kind that has passed through a statutory inspector-general channel, been assessed as credible and urgent, been transmitted to the Director of National Intelligence and both intelligence committees, and then been repeated under oath in open session with the penalty of perjury attached. The specific charge is not that craft exist; it is a financial-crimes charge -- that money appropriated by Congress for other purposes was diverted, and that the diversion was the concealment method. That reframes the question from metaphysics to auditability. Grusch's counsel is the man who built the ICIG whistleblower system, which means the filing was engineered to survive procedurally. And Grusch's own hand appears in the FY2023 NDAA UAP language, so the statutory tripwires now on the books were drafted by the complainant against the mechanism he was complaining about.
entityDossier.narrative:
Precision matters more here than anywhere else on the board, because the allegation has been repeatedly restated in forms Grusch never used.

What he filed: in May 2022, Charles McCullough III -- senior partner at Compass Rose Legal Group, and the original Inspector General of the Intelligence Community, confirmed by the Senate in 2011 under DNI James Clapper -- filed on Grusch's behalf a "Disclosure of Urgent Concern(s); Complaint of Reprisal" with the ICIG. The complaint concerned information Grusch had gathered beginning in 2019 while working with the UAP Task Force. All testimony Grusch provided for the classified complaint was given under oath, and the document closed with his signed affirmation: "I do solemnly affirm under the penalties of perjury that the contents of the foregoing paper are true and correct to the best of my knowledge."

What the unclassified version of the complaint says: that Grusch has direct knowledge that UAP-related classified information has been withheld and concealed from Congress by "elements" of the intelligence community "to purposely and intentionally thwart legitimate Congressional oversight of the UAP Program." Note the construction -- withheld from Congress, intentionally, to defeat oversight. That is an allegation about a crime against the legislature, not about biology.

What the ICIG did: found the complaint "credible and urgent" in July 2022. This is a procedural determination under the urgent-concern statute -- it means the complaint met the threshold for transmission, not that its substance was adjudicated true. Per Grusch, a summary went immediately to DNI Avril Haines, the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. A whistleblower reprisal investigation was opened. Several current members of the alleged recovery program spoke to the Inspector General's office and, per reporting, corroborated information Grusch had provided.

What he said under oath on July 26, 2023, before the House Oversight Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs. The core sentence: "I was informed in the course of my official duties of a multi-decade UAP crash retrieval and reverse engineering program to which I was denied access to those additional read-ons when I requested it." Two things are asserted and one is not. Asserted: that he was officially informed such a program exists, and that he formally requested and was denied read-on. Not asserted: that he saw craft, materials or bodies himself. Every subsequent claim of first-hand observation attributed to him is a media artifact.

On funding, Representative Jared Moskowitz asked directly. Grusch: "I will give you generalities. I can get very specific in a closed session. But misappropriation of funds and self-fund." Two mechanisms, not one. Misappropriation -- money appropriated for a stated purpose spent on another. Self-fund -- the effort generating its own revenue, presumably through the commercial exploitation of derived technology, which would place private contractors inside the financial architecture rather than merely adjacent to it.

On sourcing, asked whether he had met people with direct knowledge of non-human origin craft, he answered: "Yes. I personally interviewed those individuals." On timeline, asked when contact first occurred: "I like to use the term nonhuman. I do not like to denote origin. Keeps the aperture open both scientifically. Certainly, like I have discussed publicly, previously 1930's." On the campaign against public knowledge, in response to Representative Anna Paulina Luna, he referred to "a multi-decade, you know, campaign to disenfranchise public interest."

His pre-hearing DOPSR-cleared statements go further on the contracting angle: "Individuals on these UAP programs approached me in my official capacity and disclosed their concerns regarding a multitude of wrongdoings, such as illegal contracting against the Federal Acquisition Regulations and other criminality and the suppression of information across a qualified industrial base and academia." He also characterized the effort as a "publicly unknown Cold War for recovered and exploited physical material -- a competition with near-peer adversaries over the years to identify UAP crashes/landings and retrieve the material for exploitation/reverse engineering to garner asymmetric national defense advantages."

The corroboration that matters is Karl E. Nell's, because Nell put his name to it while identifying himself by his official role. Nell, the Army's liaison to the UAP Task Force from 2021 to 2022, said: "His assertion concerning the existence of a terrestrial arms race occurring sub-rosa over the past eighty years focused on reverse engineering technologies of unknown origin is fundamentally correct, as is the indisputable realization that at least some of these technologies of unknown origin derive from non-human intelligence." Nell also called Grusch "beyond reproach."

The institutional counter-position arrived in 2024. AARO's historical review concluded: "AARO found no empirical evidence for claims that the USG and private companies have been reverse-engineering extraterrestrial technology," and attributed the narrative "in large part" to "circular reporting from a group of individuals who believe this to be the case." AARO further asserts that "all the authentic programs have been properly notified and reported to Congress through the congressional defense and/or intelligence committees." That last sentence is a testable claim, and it is testable only against the classified annex.

As of 2026 the legal obstacle Grusch cited has formally been removed. On July 31, 2026, Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence Aaron Lukas issued memorandum ES 2026-00818 directing that prior nondisclosure agreements, oaths and commitments are waived for current and former employees and contractors speaking to AARO or to the PURSUE Task Force. The corroboration Grusch said existed in closed session is now, on paper, free to speak.

entityDossier.whatItIs: A series of encounters in and around Rendlesham Forest, Suffolk, England, in late December 1980, between the twin USAF bases RAF Bentwaters and RAF Woodbridge, in which USAF security police and, on a later night, the deputy base commander reported an unexplained illuminated object described as metallic and triangular, together with ground depressions and elevated radiation readings. The primary document is a one-page unclassified memorandum from Lt Col Charles I. Halt to the UK Ministry of Defence dated 13 January 1981 and headed "Unexplained Lights."
entityDossier.whyImplicated: Rendlesham is the cleanest specimen on the board of an official, contemporaneous, signed U.S. military document describing a landed object of unknown origin at a nuclear-capable forward base -- and of the institutional machinery that made it go away. The memo was never classified, which is itself the tell: a document that is not secret cannot be leaked, and a document that is not investigated cannot generate a record. The USAF then threw away its own copy and had to obtain another from the British MoD when a FOIA requester asked for it in 1983. On the British side, a defence minister's briefing paper concluded in writing that "no additional action was required," reasoning from Halt's two-week reporting delay and "relatively low-key manner" rather than from the physical evidence the memo describes. Rendlesham is therefore the paper trail of a non-investigation: everything that would have been generated by taking it seriously is absent, and the absence is documented.
entityDossier.narrative:
The Halt memo is short enough to quote nearly in full, and its brevity is part of the case.

Paragraph 1: "Early in the morning of 27 Dec 80 (approximately 0300L) two USAF security police patrolmen saw unusual lights outside the back gate at RAF Woodbridge. Thinking an aircraft might have crashed or been forced down, they called for permission to go outside the gate to investigate. The on-duty flight chief responded and allowed three patrolmen to proceed on foot. The individuals reported seeing a strange glowing object in the forest. The object was described as being metallic in appearance and triangular in shape, approximately two to three meters across the base and approximately two meters high. It illuminated the entire forest with a white light. The object itself had a pulsing red light on top and a bank(s) of blue lights underneath. The object was hovering or on legs. As the patrolmen approached the object, it maneuvered through the trees and disappeared. At this time the animals on a nearby farm went into a frenzy. The object was briefly sighted approximately an hour later near the back gate."

Paragraph 2: "The next day, three depressions 1.5 inches deep and 7 inches in diameter were found where the object had been sighted on the ground. The following night (29 Dec 80) the area was checked for radiation. Beta/gamma readings of 0.1 milliroentgens were recorded with peak readings in the three depressions and near the center of the triangle formed by the depressions. A nearby tree had moderate (0.05-0.07) readings on the side of the tree toward the depressions."

Paragraph 3 describes the third night: a "red sun-like light" that "appeared to throw off glowing particles and then broke into five separate white objects," then three star-like objects at about ten degrees elevation, two north and one south, moving "in sharp, angular movements" and displaying red, green and blue lights, the southern object "visible for two or three hours" and beaming "down a stream of light from time to time." Halt closes: "Numerous individuals, including the undersigned, witnessed the activities in paragraphs 2 and 3." Signed, Charles I. Halt, Lt Col, USAF, Deputy Base Commander.

This is a deputy base commander of a major forward USAF installation putting his name to a report of a landed object, physical ground traces, radiological readings taken with an instrument, and multiple military witnesses including himself. The memo was written on official USAF letterhead and was not classified in any way. It went to the British MoD. It was released under the U.S. Freedom of Information Act in June 1983 to Robert Todd of Citizens Against UFO Secrecy -- and the covering letter to Todd explains that the USAF had discarded its own copy and had to obtain another from the British MoD to satisfy the request. A U.S. Air Force base commander's report of a landed unknown craft was, by the institution's own account, not worth keeping.

The British disposition is documented with equal precision. In October 1985 the defence minister Lord David Trefgarne held a private, off-the-record meeting with Lord Peter Hill-Norton, the former Chief of the Defence Staff, who had been pressing the MoD on the case. The briefing paper prepared for Trefgarne survives as pages 115-116 of file DEFE 24/1925 at The National Archives, released in May 2008. Trefgarne's recorded view: "Our own view also was that no additional action was required. We believe that the fact that Col. Halt did not report these occurrences to MoD for almost two weeks after the event, together with the relatively low-key manner in which he handled the matter, are indicative of the degree of importance in defence terms which should be attached to the incident." The reasoning is worth isolating: the MoD assessed the significance of a reported landing not from the reported facts but from the reporter's delay and demeanour. Trefgarne wrote "Oh, dear" at the top of Hill-Norton's letter of 26 July 1985, which survives at pages 208-210 of the same file and in duplicate at pages 259-261 and 280-282 of DEFE 31/174.

Simon Weeden, the MoD desk officer who received the Halt memo, later described the disposition to journalist David Clarke: "once we had been through all the basic checks and found there was nothing seen on radar, no obvious explanation, no obvious threat to air defence, we decided no further action was needed." No witness was interviewed. No further official report was made or action taken by the U.S. or U.K. authorities beyond the memo.

In June 2010 Halt wrote and signed a two-page notarised affidavit committing his then-current memory to paper. It goes materially beyond the memo. It says one of the objects moved overhead and sent a laser-like beam down to their feet; that the same object then moved back toward Bentwaters and sent beams of light down into the Weapons Storage Area; and that several airmen present reported seeing the beams. Neither the beam-to-their-feet event nor the Weapons Storage Area beams appear in the 1981 memo or on Halt's contemporaneous field tape.

The denials attached to the affidavit are themselves catalogued artifacts. Airman Tim Egercic, on duty at the Bentwaters Weapons Storage Area, has specifically denied that any beams came down into the WSA. Halt's superior officer Col Ted Conrad, who says he was watching from outside his quarters at Woodbridge and saw nothing resembling Halt's descriptions, said of him: "He should be ashamed and embarrassed by his allegation that his country and England both conspired to deceive their citizens over this issue. He knows better." Conrad's statement is a dated, attributable denial by a named commanding officer -- which makes it evidence about the chain of command's posture, whatever it establishes about the lights.

entityDossier.narrative:
The name is an analogy, and the analogy is doing analytical work, so it is worth stating precisely what is being claimed and what is not.

What is not claimed: that a document exists bearing the title 'Manhattan Project II.' No such document has been produced. The phrase circulates in independent investigative work and podcasting, and its use there does not constitute evidence.

What is claimed, by named individuals with attributable positions: that the United States has run, since roughly the 1940s, a compartmented effort to recover and exploit materials of non-human origin, structured to be invisible to ordinary oversight, and that the Manhattan Project is the correct organisational template for understanding it. The template matters because the Manhattan Project is the canonical American precedent for a state-scale industrial programme conducted in total secrecy -- AARO's own historical review notes that in 1942 'the USG started the Manhattan Project. This program operated in secrecy and led to the establishment of several "secret cities" across the United States to support the development of the nuclear bomb.' That is the model: not a hidden filing cabinet but a hidden industrial base.

Karl E. Nell is the central named proponent. At the first symposium of the Sol Foundation, held at Stanford in November 2023, Nell called for a 'campaign plan' to force greater transparency and a 'Manhattan project' to reverse engineer recovered UAP. His presented slides set a disclosure target of October 1, 2030, acknowledged schedule risk, and listed the intended outcomes: 'Proper Oversight Restored,' 'Catastrophic Disclosure Avoid[ed],' and 'Scientific Understanding Advanced.' The operative line is his advocacy for 'restoration of proper Federal government oversight over all UAP legacy (and ongoing) program efforts.' The word 'restoration' presupposes that oversight was lost. The words 'legacy (and ongoing)' presuppose a continuous programme lineage.

Nell's credentials are not in dispute. He was the Army's liaison for the UAP Task Force from 2021 to 2022, working alongside Grusch. Lieutenant General Laura A. Potter, Deputy Chief of Staff for Intelligence, Headquarters, Department of the Army, described him in a 2022 performance evaluation as 'an officer with the strongest possible moral compass.' His most recent listed position was Modernization Advisor to the Vice Chief of Staff of the Army.

The second proponent is Hal Puthoff, the former CIA-affiliated physicist, who told the same Stanford symposium that in 2004 a CIA think tank, the Defense Intelligence Agency and the Pentagon broadly agreed that information about UFOs should not be declassified, deeming the societal risks too great. This is a reported claim about an unproduced 2004 decision, and it is tiered accordingly -- but note its structural role: it supplies a mechanism and a date for the maintenance of secrecy in the modern era rather than its origin.

The third is Grusch, who framed the same object financially and temporally: a 'publicly unknown Cold War for recovered and exploited physical material,' an 'eighty-year arms race' whose continuation in secrecy 'further inhibits the world populace to be prepared for an unexpected, non-human intelligence contact scenario.' The fourth is Jonathan Grey of the National Air and Space Intelligence Center at Wright-Patterson, who said on the record that 'the existence of complex historical programs involving the coordinated retrieval and study of exotic materials, dating back to the early 20th century, should no longer remain a secret.' The fifth is Christopher Mellon, who said officials had shared with him 'insights into the history, governing documents and the location where a craft was allegedly abandoned and recovered' -- governing documents being the phrase an analyst should mark.

The Department's counter-narrative is the KONA BLUE file, and it deserves close reading because it concedes more than it intends. AARO reports that multiple interviewees identified KONA BLUE as 'a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) sensitive compartment established to protect the retrieval and exploitation of "non-human biologics."' AARO's correction is that KONA BLUE was a Prospective Special Access Program proposed to DHS leadership, never approved, never funded, never in receipt of material. But AARO also states that in 2011 the DHS Under Secretary for Science and Technology did establish KONA BLUE as a PSAP, citing claims that relevant information and material existed and required that level of protection, and citing congressional interest and possible homeland security impacts; and that six months later the Deputy Secretary of DHS disapproved it as a SAP and directed immediate termination over the adequacy of justification and the sufficiency of information including personnel and budget requirements. So: a Cabinet department stood up a protective compartment on the represented existence of retrieved non-human material, and a Deputy Secretary killed it. That is an architecture attempting to form and being caught mid-formation.

AARO traces the proposal's lineage to AAWSAP/AATIP, managed by DIA from 2009 to 2012, funded through congressional earmarks, with Bigelow Aerospace of Nevada as prime contractor. And AARO separately concedes: 'In 2021, without sufficient justification, the scope of an IC Controlled Access Program was expanded to protect UAP reverse-engineering.'

AARO's overall verdict is flat: 'AARO found no empirical evidence for claims that the USG and private companies have been reverse-engineering extraterrestrial technology,' the narrative being 'in large part, the result of circular reporting from a group of individuals who believe this to be the case,' and 'all the authentic programs have been properly notified and reported to Congress.' AARO also reports that executives, scientists and chief technology officers of the named companies met the Director of AARO and 'denied on the record that they have ever recovered, possessed, or engaged in reverse-engineering of extraterrestrial technology.' Those denials are artifacts with dates and signatories, and they are the most specific corporate denials on the record.

entityDossier.whatItIs: Record Group 615, the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection at the U.S. National Archives, created by Sections 1841-1843 of the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act (Public Law 118-31, div. A, title XVIII, subtitle C, December 22, 2023, 137 Stat. 699). It is the statutory destination for record copies of all Government, Government-provided or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: RG 615 is the first time Congress has created a records collection whose statutory scope explicitly includes 'technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence.' A legislature does not write a records-collection statute around a category it believes to be empty; the statutory text is itself a congressional finding that such records are believed to exist and to be held by federal agencies. But the enforcement architecture was hollowed. The Senate-origin design contemplated an independent review board to push postponed records toward disclosure; the enacted subtitle contains none. Postponement is decided by 'the original classification authority' -- the agency holding the record -- and postponed records physically remain with the originating body until NARA stands up a security programme. So the collection that was supposed to break the compartment is, for the withheld portion, still inside the compartment. What has actually arrived at RG 615 by 2026 is the readily releasable material from FAA, NRC, ODNI, OSD, NSA, State and FBI, joined on 28 August 2026 by the first military department to transfer in its own right: thirty unrestricted Air Force PDFs from 1945 to 1969.
entityDossier.narrative:
Read the statute rather than the coverage.

Section 1841(a)(1)(A) required the Archivist to commence establishing the collection within 60 days of enactment. Section 1841(a)(1)(C) defines its contents with unusual reach: 'record copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence (or equivalent subjects by any other name with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects).' Three features of that sentence are load-bearing. First, 'Government-funded' reaches contractor holdings. Second, 'or equivalent subjects by any other name' is an anti-euphemism clause -- a direct legislative anticipation that the material will be filed under cover terminology. Third, the sole carve-out is for temporarily non-attributed objects, i.e. drones and balloons, which is Congress saying the collection is not about the prosaic.

Section 1841(a)(1)(D) requires the Archivist to 'prepare and publish a subject guidebook and index to the Collection.' Section 1841(b) requires that transmitted records be available for inspection and copying at the National Archives within 30 days of transmission and digitally within not more than 180 days thereafter. Section 1841(e) assigns continuing oversight jurisdiction to Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, Armed Services and Intelligence, and to House Oversight and Accountability, Armed Services and Intelligence.

Section 1842 governs the agencies. Subsection (c)(1) gave each head of a Government office 300 days from December 22, 2023 to review, identify and organise every UAP record in its custody for disclosure and transmission. Subsection (a)(2)(A) is absolute: 'No unidentified anomalous phenomena record shall be destroyed, altered, or mutilated in any way.' Subsection (a)(2)(B) forbids withholding, redacting, postponing or reclassifying any UAP record already made available or disclosed to the public before enactment -- a retroactive lock on the existing public record, including documents like the Halt memo. Subsection (a)(2)(C) extends the same protection to records created by persons or entities outside the federal government.

Subsection (c)(2)(G) sets priorities, and the priority order is revealing. Agencies must give precedence first to records not already public; second to 'all records that most unambiguously and definitively pertain to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence'; third to records already in FOIA litigation; fourth to earliest-provenance records. Congress wrote a triage rule that puts the most explicitly non-human material at the front of the queue.

Then the gate. Section 1843(a) permits postponement 'if the original classification authority makes a determination that there is clear and convincing evidence' that the threat to military defence, intelligence operations or foreign relations 'is of such gravity that it outweighs the public interest in disclosure' and that disclosure would reveal a currently protected agent, a currently used source or method, or 'any other matter currently relating to the military defense, intelligence operations, or conduct of foreign relations of the United States, the disclosure of which would demonstrably and substantially impair the national security.' Additional grounds cover the Privacy Act, unwarranted invasion of personal privacy, and confidentiality understandings with cooperating individuals.

'Clear and convincing evidence' is a demanding standard on paper. The problem is who applies it. The original classification authority is an official of the agency that owns the record and, on the allegations at issue, may be the same institutional actor accused of the concealment. There is no independent adjudicator in the enacted text. This is the JFK Records Act model with the Assassination Records Review Board removed.

Section 1842(g) supplies the only ongoing pressure. Postponed records must be reviewed periodically by the originating agency and the Archivist. Every continued postponement 'shall require an unclassified written description of the reason for such continued postponement relevant to these specific records,' provided to the Archivist and published in the Federal Register. And section 1842(g)(2)(D) sets the backstop: each record must be publicly disclosed in full not later than 25 years after its first creation, unless the President personally certifies that continued postponement is necessitated by an identifiable harm of such gravity that it outweighs the public interest. On a 25-year rule, anything created before 2001 is already past due absent a presidential certification.

Section 1841(d)(2) and section 1842(f) together create the physical bottleneck. NARA's National Security Program Office, with the Information Security Oversight Office, must establish a programme to secure the postponed and classified portion of the collection -- and until that programme exists, postponed records are 'held for reasons of security and preservation by the originating body.' The withheld material does not move.

What has actually landed is documented on NARA's RG 615 page: series from the Federal Aviation Administration (National Archives Identifier 493468575), the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (488808322), the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (493468579), the Office of the Secretary of Defense (493468580), the National Security Agency (580103959), the Department of State (608806625), and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (580705010) -- seven as of the page's May 22, 2026 review date -- and, added on August 28, 2026, the Department of the Air Force (656595571).

The Air Force series is the first transfer by a military department in its own right, and it is worth reading closely because it is the only evidence on the board of what compliance looks like when an agency with custody proximity actually does it. It is accession TR-0615-2026-0003: thirty PDF files, inclusive dates 25 October 1945 to 31 December 1969, access and use both Unrestricted, disposition authority DAA-GRS-2024-0002-0001, described from NARA file NAC_2026-08-27_23.116_DESC_0001.xml and indexed at 08:30 UTC on 28 August 2026. The thirty items carry contiguous UAP Record Identifiers 342UAP00001 to 342UAP00030 and each has one attached PDF; all thirty were fetched and returned PDF content.

Two things about the contents matter more than the count. The first is the declassification block printed on the documents themselves. Item 342UAP00005 carries 'Air Force Declassification Office / Authority: FY24 NDAA, now codified at 44 U.S.C. 2107 / Date: 5/05/2025 / Declassified in Full: X / Case Number: 342UAP00005'. The Air Force ran this as a declassification action under the UAP records statute, in May 2025, and used the UAP Record Identifier as its own case number -- so the identifier series is a declassification docket, and the gap between the May 2025 decision and the August 2026 accession is over fifteen months of something other than review.

The second is that the titles cannot be taken at face value. Item 342UAP00005 is catalogued as 'Estimate of the Situation, September 8, 1948', which reads as the Air Materiel Command estimate that Ruppelt described and that Vandenberg is said to have ordered destroyed. It is not. Opened, it is Headquarters Fifth Air Force, Office of the AC of S, A-2, APO 710, a 21-page periodic Far East theatre intelligence estimate covering 7 August to 4 September 1948, published for Fifth Air Force Division and Wing-Base Commanders, whose table of contents runs Japan, Korea, China, Philippines, Malaya. Eighteen of the thirty items are unit or installation histories of the same kind, in which any UAP content is a passage inside a monthly wing or division history rather than the subject of the document. Anyone citing this series from its catalog titles will misdescribe it. NARA issued AC Memo 04.2025 to agencies on the transfer of publicly releasable UAP records, and describes transfers as arriving on a rolling basis.

By 2026 a parallel executive channel has opened alongside the statutory one. Following a presidential order to disclose collected UAP records, the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters -- the PURSUE Task Force -- released a fourth tranche of records on July 10, 2026, published at war.gov/ufo, and ODNI issued memorandum ES 2026-00818 on July 31, 2026 waiving nondisclosure agreements for anyone speaking to PURSUE or AARO. The analytically important question is whether PURSUE releases are being routed into RG 615 as section 1842(e) requires, or are accumulating in a separate executive-branch publication stream outside the Archivist's custody and outside the Federal Register accountability of section 1842(g)(2)(B).

claims.text: Record Group 615, the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection, was created by Sections 1841-1843 of the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act, Public Law 118-31, div. A, title XVIII, subtitle C, December 22, 2023, 137 Stat. 699.

claims.text: Section 1841(a)(1)(C) provides that the Collection 'shall consist of record copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence (or equivalent subjects by any other name with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects).'

Section 1842(c)(1) required each head of a Government office to review, identify and organise every UAP record in its custody for public disclosure and transmission to the Archivist not later than 300 days after December 22, 2023.
Section 1842(a)(2)(A) provides that 'No unidentified anomalous phenomena record shall be destroyed, altered, or mutilated in any way.'
Section 1842(a)(2)(B) bars any UAP record made available or disclosed to the public before December 22, 2023 from being withheld, redacted, postponed for public disclosure, or reclassified.

Section 1842(c)(2)(G)(ii) directs agencies to give precedence to 'the identification, review, and transmission of all records that most unambiguously and definitively pertain to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence.'

Section 1843(a) permits postponement of disclosure only where 'the original classification authority makes a determination that there is clear and convincing evidence' of enumerated harms; the enacted subtitle establishes no independent review board to adjudicate those determinations.

Section 1842(g)(2)(B) requires that every continued postponement carry 'an unclassified written description of the reason for such continued postponement relevant to these specific records,' provided to the Archivist and published in the Federal Register.

Section 1842(g)(2)(D) requires each UAP record to be publicly disclosed in full not later than 25 years after its first creation unless the President certifies that continued postponement is made necessary by an identifiable harm whose gravity outweighs the public interest in disclosure.

Section 1841(d)(2) requires NARA's National Security Program Office, with the Information Security Oversight Office, to establish a security programme for postponed records, and section 1842(f) provides that postponed records are held by the originating body until that programme exists -- so withheld records physically remain with the agency that withheld them.

entityDossier.denialPosture: No agency has publicly asserted that it holds no UAP records; the posture is instead procedural. Agencies transfer 'publicly releasable' material under AC Memo 04.2025 while postponement determinations remain with each originating agency's own original classification authority under section 1843(a), and postponed records stay physically in agency custody under section 1842(f) pending a NARA security programme. The result is that the withholding is never articulated as a denial -- it is expressed as a classification determination made by the withholder.
connections: RG 615 is the disclosure end-state of the same statutory sequence that begins with 50 U.S.C. 3373b (FY2023 NDAA sec. 1673), which Grusch helped draft.
Section 1843's 'original classification authority' gate imports the self-adjudication principle described in classified-annex.
Records like the Halt memo and the DEFE 24 files bearing on rendlesham-1980 fall under section 1842(a)(2)(B)'s bar on re-withholding already-public UAP records.

AARO is named in sections 1842(c)(2)(E), (F) and (3) as an office that other agencies must make records available to -- giving the office accused of being non-neutral a statutory role in the records pipeline.
The KONA BLUE and AAWSAP/AATIP documents released by DoD and DHS in partnership are precisely the class of record section 1842 was written to capture.
The 2026 PURSUE Task Force and ODNI memorandum ES 2026-00818 (Aaron Lukas, July 31, 2026) run alongside RG 615 and raise the question of dual custody.
Presidential libraries and archival depositories under 44 U.S.C. 2112 are given expedited-review priority by section 1842(c)(3), reaching back into the 1944-1970 period this board covers.

entityDossier.whatItIs: DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs (SAPs),' signed by the Deputy Secretary of Defense and effective February 6, 2013, cancelling the classified DoDI 0-5205.11 of July 1, 1997. It is the unclassified, publicly releasable rulebook for how the Department creates, nests, staffs, reports, waives reporting on, and disestablishes special access programs, and it implements the congressional oversight statute at 10 U.S.C. 119.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: This is the machine's operating manual, published in the open, and it describes every capability a concealed legacy programme would need. It defines the unacknowledged SAP, whose very existence is not acknowledged to anyone not cleared for it. It defines the waived SAP, for which the Secretary of Defense has set aside the reporting Congress imposed. It builds a four-level nesting hierarchy -- umbrella, compartment, sub-compartment, project -- and expressly contemplates unacknowledged waived sub-elements added underneath a non-waived umbrella, which is a documented mechanism for hiding a black effort inside a program Congress has already been told about. It authorises 'carve-out' proposals to relieve the Defense Security Service of industrial security oversight over contractor performance. And it conditions access not merely on need-to-know and clearance but on a determination that the individual 'will clearly and materially contribute to the execution or oversight of the program' -- the discretionary gate through which David Grusch's read-on request was denied.
entityDossier.narrative:
The most useful thing about DoDI 5205.11 is that it is unclassified and approved for public release with unlimited releasability. The Department published its own concealment architecture and nobody read it.

Start with the vocabulary, because the Glossary is where the load is carried. An 'unacknowledged SAP' is 'A SAP having enhanced security measures ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized for such information.' A 'waived SAP' is 'A SAP for which the SecDef has waived applicable reporting ... following a determination of adverse effect to national security. An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs.' A 'waiver' more generally is 'A decision that provides an approved exception to or deviation from a SAP security standard.' Two of the three definitions describe subtraction from the oversight baseline.

The waiver traces to statute. 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) lets the Secretary of Defense waive any requirement that certain information be included in a SAP report where inclusion 'would adversely affect the national security,' case by case; 119(e)(2) routes the withheld content and the justification 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' Twelve members. No staff named. That is the entire congressional footprint of a waived SAP.

The governance layer is three committees stacked above the Deputy Secretary: the SAP Oversight Committee (SAPOC), the Senior Review Group (SRG), and the SAP Senior Working Group (SSWG), which 'advise and assist the SecDef and DepSecDef in the management, administration, and oversight of DoD SAPs.' The SRG 'Reviews all waived DoD SAPs annually' and provides recommendations to the SAPOC 'concerning continued waived status.' There is, in other words, an internal annual re-authorisation cycle for programmes Congress cannot see -- run entirely by the Department.

Establishment is the part that looks like oversight. The SAPOC reviews the package and submits it to the Deputy Secretary of Defense for decision. 'If approved, the DepSecDef will submit formal notification letters to Congress that the SAP has been established.' And: 'The SAP may not be initiated until the congressional defense committees are notified of the program and a period of 30 days has elapsed after such notification is received.' That mirrors 10 U.S.C. 119(f). The Instruction also fixes the annual reporting calendar: SAP Listing on February 1, SAP Annual Report on March 1, forwarded to the congressional defense committees by the DoD SAPCO. Those dates correspond to 10 U.S.C. 119(b) and 119(a) respectively -- and both of those statutory reporting requirements were terminated effective December 31, 2021 by section 1061 of Public Law 114-328. The Instruction's reporting calendar survives on paper; the statutory obligation behind it does not.

Now the nesting. Enclosure 5 sets out the SAP hierarchy: a SAP is called an 'umbrella' if it has subordinate elements, which in descending order are compartments, sub-compartments, and projects. A person accessed to a compartment is also accessed to all subordinate elements 'unless an exception is specifically approved by the CA SAPCO.' Subordinate elements 'will be presumed to be within the same type unless' otherwise designated -- and the Instruction expressly addresses the case of unacknowledged waived sub-elements added under a non-waived umbrella, requiring specific SAPCO action. Read that as an analyst: the doctrine anticipates, and provides procedure for, burying a waived unacknowledged effort inside a programme that has been properly reported. This is the documented, unclassified mechanism corresponding exactly to Grusch's charge of 'nesting UAP activities in conventional SAP/CAP programs ... without appropriate reporting to various oversight authorities.'

Enclosure 6 lists what a Cognizant Authority SAPCO must notify the Director, DoD SAPCO of in writing. The list is a taxonomy of the moves available: change of category (acquisition, intelligence, operations and support); 'Change of type (acknowledged, unacknowledged)'; 'Alteration of scope'; IJSTO apportionment or deapportionment; disestablishment by termination, cancellation or transition; 'Support of non-DoD SAPs'; 'Addition, deletion, or changes of compartments, sub-compartments, and projects'; 'Proposals to relieve DSS of NISP security oversight responsibilities (carve-out) when required'; 'Change of nickname, codeword, PID'; and 'Foreign involvement.' Every one of these is an entry point for an analyst. Nickname and codeword changes break longitudinal tracking. Carve-outs remove the Defense Security Service from contractor facilities. 'Support of non-DoD SAPs' is the doctrinal bridge to DHS, DOE and IC compartments -- the category KONA BLUE would have occupied had it been approved.

Access is the human gate. 'Access to a SAP will be strictly limited to the minimum number of personnel necessary for execution of the program. Granting access to a SAP will be based solely upon a determination that the individual has a valid NTK, has the requisite security clearance, meets approved personnel prerequisites, and will clearly and materially contribute to the execution or oversight of the program.' The final clause is a subjective judgment reserved to the programme, and it is the clause that answers Grusch's testimony that he was 'denied access to those additional read-ons when I requested it.' Under this Instruction, a person conducting oversight can be lawfully excluded on the programme's own determination that he would not materially contribute to it.

Two further details reward attention. Sample SAP approval documentation reproduced in the Instruction's appendices uses a notional unacknowledged operations-and-support SAP designated GTE, with planned unacknowledged sub-compartments including LEAF BARK (LBK) and a recommendation line reading 'That you approve GTE as an unacknowledged SAP and authorize' -- a published template showing exactly how a sub-compartment request is written and approved. And the Instruction carries its own expiry: it 'Must be reissued, cancelled, or certified current within 5 years of its publication ... If not it will expire effective February 6, 2023.'

The Instruction contains a self-expiry clause: it 'Must be reissued, cancelled, or certified current within 5 years of its publication in accordance with DoDI 5025.01. If not it will expire effective February 6, 2023 and be removed from the DoD Issuances Website.'

entityDossier.denialPosture: None. DoDI 5205.11 asserts nothing about UAP and denies nothing; it is a procedural issuance published with unlimited releasability. Its evidentiary value is that the Department has openly documented, in its own doctrine, every structural capability -- unacknowledged type, waived reporting, nested waived sub-elements under reported umbrellas, industrial-security carve-outs, and discretionary denial of oversight read-ons -- that a concealed legacy programme would require.
connections: Implements 10 U.S.C. 119, the statute whose subsection (e) waiver and December 31, 2021 reporting termination are the core of classified-annex.
The 'will clearly and materially contribute to the execution or oversight of the program' access gate is the doctrinal basis for the read-on denial David Grusch testified to on July 26, 2023.

'Support of non-DoD SAPs' is the doctrinal bridge to the DHS compartment KONA BLUE would have become, and to the IC Controlled Access Program AARO says was expanded in 2021 to protect UAP reverse-engineering.

The carve-out provision relieving the Defense Security Service of National Industrial Security Program oversight is the mechanism by which contractor facilities performing SAP work fall outside routine DoD industrial security inspection.
'Change of nickname, codeword, PID' is the doctrinal answer to why a legacy effort would be untrackable across decades even to cleared reviewers.
The February 1 SAP Listing and March 1 SAP Annual Report are the documents that, if they still existed, would settle whether an unreported UAP materials programme is inside the DoD SAP inventory.
Deputy Secretary of Defense signature authority makes the DepSecDef, not the SecDef, the approving official for SAP establishment -- a specific office to interrogate for any given programme's origin.
